title: Professor Helen X. H. Bao
notes:
Moodle version of Week 7, built on 2026-10-26 from the Week 1 Moodle deck as the format template, in the way Weeks 2 and 3 were built. 23 slides against the 30 asked for. The earlier 65-slide deck is kept beside it (RE07 Week 7 - Sustainability ESG and Emerging Trends.pptx) as the source of material; it is untouched and still describes the earlier shape of the week, which was organised around the letters E, S and G and a block on spatial finance.

SHAPE OF THE DECK

The first hour is broad and the second hour zooms in. Five survey parts, each at most two or three slides and each anchored in a paper or report that I actually read: measuring sustainability (2 slides), climate and water risk in prices (3), carbon and green labels in asset prices (2), disclosure and supervision (2), and data centres and the environment (2). The focus part (8 slides) is one question seen through three models with an interactive page each: what the market pays for sustainability, how a distant benefit is discounted, and what a protection measure earns in avoided losses. The pages open on generic settings. Then the case (1 slide, headings only) and the summary. There is no thank-you slide.

WHY THE FOCUS IS NOT WATER

The case is on water infrastructure and the environmental dimension of ESG, and it is one case. The first hour is therefore not about water. The focus models are general (a sustainability preference in prices, long-horizon discounting, protection against rare losses), and each of them is something a water case can test. Water appears in the survey where the literature puts it: as one of the categories raters disagree on (slide 4), in the Aqueduct indicators (slide 6), in the financial stability agenda (slide 11), and in the reporting of data centres (slide 13 notes).

DATA CENTRES

The week's aspect of the course thread on data centres is the environmental one: who bears the damage (slide 13) and when flexible load helps the grid and when it does not (slide 14). Scale and booms belong to Week 1, local incidence and the grid to Week 2, financing to Week 3, and these slides do not repeat them.

WHAT TO ASK ANDY

Every first-hour slide ends its notes with a section headed WHAT TO ASK ANDY, naming the evidence his case could supply for that slide, and the case slide holds the consolidated list in priority order. Every focus slide ends with RETURN TO THIS IN THE CASE.

PAGE NUMBERS AND WHAT IS NOT VERIFIED

Every source is cited in the notes of its slide with page numbers, which are the printed page numbers of the version I read and which each note names. Several are working papers: Berg, Koelbel and Rigobon is the August 2019 MIT Sloan working paper (five raters; the published Review of Finance version has, I recall, a sixth rater and lower correlations, which I have not checked); Pastor, Stambaugh and Taylor is NBER Working Paper 26549; Bolton and Kacperczyk is NBER 26968; Baker and co-authors is NBER 25194; Giglio, Kelly and Stroebel is NBER 28226; Muller and Knittel and co-authors are NBER working papers from 2026 and 2025. Not retrieved: Weitzman (2001), Painter (2020) and Bernstein and co-authors (2019), which are used second-hand through Giglio and co-authors; the OECD publication Embedding Water-related Risks in Financial Stability Frameworks (the OECD page returned an access error); and IFRS S2, whose download was a sign-in page, so the disclosure slide uses the TCFD report of June 2017. The Lifelines booklet is the pre-publication overview. The February 2026 Green Book guidance is HM Treasury policy; the June 2026 review by Freeman and Groom is independent and is not.

title: ESG Ratings Disagree
notes:
THE FIGURE

Berg, Koelbel and Rigobon (2019), Table 2, printed page 7: the correlations between the ESG ratings of five raters (KLD, Sustainalytics, Vigeo-Eiris, RobecoSAM and Asset4) on a common sample of firms, for the ten pairs of raters. The bars are averages of the ten pairs and the line runs from the lowest to the highest pair. Computed from the table: environmental 0.64, social 0.49, governance 0.43, ESG overall 0.61 (0.42 to 0.73). The bottom bar is the correlation between Moody's and Standard and Poor's credit ratings, 0.994 (introduction, page 2).

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

The authors estimate that about USD 30 trillion of assets are invested relying in some way on ESG ratings (page 2). The correlation between raters is on average 0.61, against 0.99 for the two credit rating agencies, and the paper draws three consequences: ESG performance is unlikely to be properly reflected in prices, because the divergence disperses the effect of investors' tastes; firms receive mixed signals; and empirical studies can change their result with the choice of rater (page 2). That first consequence is the link to the focus model of the hour. A taste for green assets can only move prices if enough investors agree on which assets are green.

CAUTIONS

The text of the paper prints 0.65 as the average for the environmental dimension and 0.38 for governance (page 7); the table gives 0.64 and 0.43 when I average its ten pairs. I plotted the table and the discrepancy is small, but check against the published version before quoting a figure. The text also gives the credit-rating correlation as 0.994 in the introduction and as 98.6 per cent in section 3.1 (page 7), an internal inconsistency in the working paper. This is the August 2019 working paper with five raters. I recall that the published version (Review of Finance, 2022) adds a sixth rater and reports an average near 0.54; I have not checked it.

SOURCE

Berg, F., Koelbel, J. F. and Rigobon, R. (2019), Aggregate confusion: the divergence of ESG ratings, MIT Sloan Working Paper 5822-19, 15 August 2019, pages 2 and 7 (printed page equals PDF page less one).

WHAT TO ASK ANDY

Request 7. Whether the assets or institutions in his case carry an ESG score, a rating or a labelled-instrument status, from whom, and whether raters disagree about them. If his case has an investor or lender with a sustainability screen, the page that matters is how that screen treats water.

title: Sources of Rating Divergence
notes:
THE FIGURE

Berg, Koelbel and Rigobon (2019), introduction, pages 3 and 4: the divergence between the ratings of two raters is split into measurement (the same category scored differently), scope (different sets of categories) and weight (different importance given to each category), by a regression on a common taxonomy of 64 categories. Measurement 53 per cent, scope 44 per cent, weight 3 per cent.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

The paper first shows that each rater's aggregate rule can be approximated by a linear weighted average of category scores with an accuracy above 90 per cent (page 3). Its second result is the split shown. Its third, and the one that matters for a sector such as water, is that divergence grows with granularity: the correlations between raters in individual categories are well below those for the aggregate, and the water category, scored by all five raters (with between 1 and 3 indicators each, Table 4), has an average correlation of 0.33 across the ten pairs, between 0.12 and 0.47 (Table 5, page 18), against 0.29 for energy. The authors also detect a rater effect, in which a rater's view of the whole firm influences its score in individual categories (abstract, page 1).

CAUTIONS

The split depends on the method. The arithmetic decomposition in section 5.1.1 gives measurement 47, scope 29 and weight 24 per cent of the absolute variation (page 25), and the authors say it is not a proper variance decomposition. Use the regression-based split as the headline and say so. The data are firm-level ratings of listed companies, and a project or a utility is not a listed company; the categories are the ones a rater applies to firms.

SOURCE

Berg, Koelbel and Rigobon (2019), MIT Sloan Working Paper 5822-19, pages 1, 3 to 4, 18 and 25, Tables 4 and 5 (printed page equals PDF page less one).

WHAT TO ASK ANDY

Request 7 again, narrowly. Whether he can say how rating providers and lenders score water risk for the sector in his case, and whether the scores diverge in the way the water category does. One concrete example of two providers scoring the same asset differently would serve this slide better than any aggregate.

title: Climate Risk in Long-Dated Asset Prices
notes:
THE TABLE

Three results from the survey of climate finance by Giglio, Kelly and Stroebel (NBER Working Paper 28226, December 2020), set out by asset. The first two are reported by the survey from other papers, which I did not retrieve.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

Coastal homes. Bernstein and co-authors (2019) find that properties inundated after one foot of global average sea-level rise sell at a 14.7 per cent discount, those inundated with two to three feet at 13.8 per cent, and those inundated with six feet at 4.4 per cent (pages 22 and 23). The discount is largest for the homes that flood first and falls to 4.4 per cent for those that flood only at six feet, which suggests that the market prices the nearer and likelier exposure and discounts the far tail. That reading is mine, not the survey's.

Municipal bonds. Painter (2020) shows that at-issuance municipal bond yields are higher for counties with large expected losses from sea-level rise, and that the effect is concentrated in long-dated bonds and essentially absent at short maturities. Goldsmith-Pinkham and co-authors (2019) translate the yield effect into a 3 to 8 per cent reduction in the present value of local governments' long-run cash flows (page 16). This is the link between the climate evidence and the discounting model later in the hour: physical risk shows up at long maturities.

Discount rates. The survey explains why the sign of the risk premium on investments that mitigate climate damage is disputed. If the uncertainty is about the climate itself, mitigation and hedging assets pay off in bad states and carry negative risk premia, so they should be discounted below the risk-free rate. If the uncertainty is about the path of the economy, such investments pay off when marginal utility is low and carry positive premia (pages 7 to 9). The authors say the evidence on the term structure favours the climate-disaster version with partial recovery. The June 2026 review of the Green Book reaches a related place by a different road, with a negative risk premium for projects that pay off in times of societal decline (slide 18).

CAUTIONS

Giglio and co-authors say that a second challenge is that climate risk may be priced today but is hard to detect, because it evolves slowly (page 14). The housing figures are discounts for exposure to sea-level rise in US coastal markets and say nothing about water scarcity or inland flooding. Neither Bernstein nor Painter nor Goldsmith-Pinkham was retrieved. Check the figures in the originals before quoting them in print.

SOURCE

Giglio, S., Kelly, B. and Stroebel, J. (2020), Climate finance, NBER Working Paper 28226, pages 7 to 9, 16, 22 and 23 (printed page equals PDF page less one). Prepared for the Annual Review of Financial Economics.

WHAT TO ASK ANDY

Request 7 and Request 4. Whether any price in his case reflects physical water risk, for example a spread, a valuation discount, an insurance premium or a lender condition, and over what maturity. Failing that, whether the asset's cash flows are long-dated enough that the pattern in slide 5 would be expected to show.

title: Water Risk Indicators
notes:
THE TABLE

The thresholds for the baseline water stress indicator in Aqueduct 4.0 (Kuzma and co-authors, WRI Technical Note, August 2023, page 11). Baseline water stress is the ratio of total water demand (domestic, industrial, irrigation and livestock, consumptive and non-consumptive) to available renewable surface and groundwater supplies; higher values indicate more competition among users. The raw value is converted to a risk category and a score from 0 to 5 using thresholds taken from Aqueduct 2.1 (Gassert and co-authors, 2014): below 10 per cent low (0 to 1), 10 to 20 low-medium (1 to 2), 20 to 40 medium-high (2 to 3), 40 to 80 high (3 to 4), above 80 extremely high (4 to 5); sub-basins classified as arid and low water use are handled separately.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

The framework has three levels: 13 indicators covering water quantity, quality and reputational risk, grouped into three groups, and combined into one overall score (pages 1 and 2). Aqueduct 4.0 uses the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction terms hazard, exposure and vulnerability and assigns each indicator one of the three risk elements (page 10); the card for the baseline water stress indicator records its risk element as R = H x E x V (page 11). The model behind five of the indicators is a global hydrological model, PCR-GLOBWB 2, and the note provides projections for 2030, 2050 and 2080 under three scenarios (abstract). The slide is there for two reasons. It shows that a risk score is a chain of choices (a unit, a threshold, a score), and slide 4 showed what happens when raters make different choices. It also supplies the hazard-exposure-vulnerability decomposition behind the loss curve in the third model.

CAUTIONS

The indicators are physical risk indicators at sub-basin scale, designed for corporate screening and for decision-makers who lack hydrological expertise; they do not value a loss and say nothing about one asset's exposure. Thresholds are borrowed from the earlier version. The note lists its limitations in a section of its own (page 36).

SOURCE

Kuzma, S., Bierkens, M. F. P., Lakshman, S., Luo, T., Saccoccia, L., Sutanudjaja, E. H. and Van Beek, R. (2023), Aqueduct 4.0: updated decision-relevant global water risk indicators, WRI Technical Note, August 2023, pages 1 to 2, 10 and 11 (printed page equals PDF page for page 11; confirm pages 1, 2 and 10 against the printed copy).

WHAT TO ASK ANDY

Request 3. Which hazard data the case uses for water (indicator, provider, scenario, period, spatial unit), and whether Aqueduct or another tool supplied it. If the data are proprietary, a description of the scale and of how the score maps to a decision is enough.

title: The Cost of Disrupted Infrastructure
notes:
THE FIGURE

Hallegatte, Rentschler and Rozenberg (2019), Lifelines, Overview, page 12: a set of 3,000 scenarios covering the uncertainty of all parameters of the analysis was used to explore the costs and benefits of making infrastructure in low and middle income countries more resilient. The benefit-cost ratio of strengthening exposed infrastructure assets is higher than 1 in 96 per cent of the scenarios, larger than 2 in 77 per cent and higher than 6 in 25 per cent. The net present value over the lifetime of new assets exceeds USD 2 trillion in 75 per cent of the scenarios and USD 4.2 trillion in half of them. Without climate change the median benefit-cost ratio would be 2, and it doubles when climate change is considered.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

Disruption to infrastructure costs households and firms in low and middle income countries at least USD 390 billion a year (page vii). The extra cost of building resilience into new infrastructure is 3 per cent of overall investment needs, and the net benefit of the investment over the life of new infrastructure would be USD 4.2 trillion, a USD 4 benefit for each dollar invested in resilience (page vii). The ratio varies so widely across scenarios that the report declines to give one estimate. It also finds that a decade of inaction is costly in 93 per cent of scenarios, with a median cost of USD 1 trillion (page 12), and that the cost of resilience can be reduced by working at the level of networks and services as well as assets (page 12). The slide gives a reference range for the third focus model, which is a calculation of the same kind with illustrative numbers.

CAUTIONS

The booklet is the overview taken from the forthcoming book and says to use the final version for citation. The figures are for new infrastructure in low and middle income countries in four sectors and rest on the study's own damage and cost assumptions. Disruption costs of USD 390 billion a year are described as at least that amount.

SOURCE

Hallegatte, S., Rentschler, J. and Rozenberg, J. (2019), Lifelines: the resilient infrastructure opportunity, World Bank, Overview, pages vii and 12 (printed pages of the overview booklet). doi 10.1596/978-1-4648-1430-3.

WHAT TO ASK ANDY

Request 4. Estimates of what disruption to water supply or treatment costs in the setting of the case, as a loss per event, per day of outage or per scenario, and who bears it. A single worked loss figure for a stated event is worth more to the third model than any range.

title: The Carbon Premium in Stock Returns
notes:
THE FIGURE

Bolton and Kacperczyk (2020), introduction, page 6 and Table 8 discussion, page 18: the annualised increase in stock returns from a one-standard-deviation increase in a firm's emissions, after controlling for size, book-to-market, momentum and other predictors. Level of emissions: scope 1, 1.8 per cent (15 basis points a month); scope 2, 2.9 per cent (24 basis points); scope 3, 4.0 per cent (33 basis points). Change in emissions: scope 1, 3.1 per cent (26 basis points); scope 2, 2.2 per cent (18 basis points); scope 3, 3.8 per cent (31 basis points).

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

The abstract states the result plainly: stocks of firms with higher total CO2 emissions, and with larger changes in emissions, earn higher returns, and the premium cannot be explained by unexpected profitability or other known risk factors (page 1). Emission intensity, the measure most widely used for exclusionary screening, has no significant effect on returns (page 6). Institutional investors do hold a significantly smaller share of firms with high scope 1 intensity, and insurance companies, pension funds and mutual funds are underweight, but they are not underweight firms with high levels of emissions (page 6). The authors call this a somewhat schizophrenic attitude: divestment is concentrated in oil and gas, utilities and motor industries, while the premium is found at firm level in all industries (page 7). The premium has only appeared recently, since there is none in the 1990s when the emissions distribution is imputed backwards (pages 7 and 8). The sign is the opposite of the one in the focus model, and the slide sets it up: a premium for emissions means high emitters are priced to earn more, which is what a market with a taste for green holdings predicts for brown assets.

CAUTIONS

The premium is a statement about US listed firms from 2005 onwards in the authors' sample and cannot be read across to infrastructure assets, many of which are unlisted. It says the market demands compensation for carbon risk. It does not say whether the compensation is correct, or whether it comes from the taste effect of the focus model or from risk; the authors lean towards risk (page 1). Scope 3 emissions are estimated and not reported by most firms. This is the April 2020 NBER version.

SOURCE

Bolton, P. and Kacperczyk, M. (2020), Do investors care about carbon risk? NBER Working Paper 26968, April 2020, pages 1, 6 to 8 and 18 (printed page equals PDF page less one).

WHAT TO ASK ANDY

Request 7. Whether the asset or its owner has a carbon dimension that investors or lenders price, for instance energy intensity of water treatment or desalination, and whether any of the parties require disclosure of scope 1 and 2 emissions. This also links to the data-centre slides, since desalination and cooling both draw on power.
text: The Carbon Premium in Stock Returns 4 The premium: firms with higher emissions earn higher returns, after the usual controls The size: one standard deviation of scope 1 adds 1.8 per cent a year, and of scope 3 adds 4.0 per cent Intensity: emission intensity, the usual screening measure, has no significant effect Timing: no premium appears in the 1990s, so awareness matters Bolton and Kacperczyk (2020), NBER Working Paper 26968, pages 1 and 6 to 8, and Table 8 discussion, page 18. title: The Green Bond Premium
notes:
THE FIGURE

Baker, Bergstresser, Serafeim and Wurgler (2018), NBER Working Paper 25194. After-tax yield at issue below an otherwise similar ordinary municipal bond, in basis points: about 6 for a bond labelled green and confirmed by Bloomberg (introduction, page 2; five to seven across specifications, page 17); 26 for a bond certified as green by a third party and registered with the Climate Bonds Initiative in the first specification, and 15 with issuer fixed effects (page 18).

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

The paper starts from a framework in which a subset of investors derive nonpecuniary utility from holding green bonds, so that expected returns have the usual CAPM term plus a term for the security's environmental score. The prediction is that green securities are priced at a premium and earn lower returns, which is the model of the focus part of the hour in a single market (page 2). They find it: on a bond with a 10-year duration a 6 basis point difference in yield is a 0.60 percentage point difference in value (page 3), which they say is as if the bond were rated half a notch higher, since an extra notch in their sample is about 12 basis points (page 17). The premium doubles or triples for certified bonds (page 3), and green bonds, particularly small or essentially riskless ones, are more closely held than ordinary bonds (abstract, page 1).

CAUTIONS

The data are US municipal and corporate green bonds up to the paper's sample date, and the premium is small in basis points. Greenness is not assigned at random, so the authors say the extent of causality cannot be pinpointed (page 18). A certified premium that falls from 26 to 15 basis points when issuer effects are added says the premium is partly a feature of who issues. Whether the premium is large enough to change the economics of a project is a separate question from whether it exists, and a 6 basis point difference is small beside the discounting choices on slide 18.

SOURCE

Baker, M., Bergstresser, D., Serafeim, G. and Wurgler, J. (2018), Financing the response to climate change: the pricing and ownership of US green bonds, NBER Working Paper 25194, October 2018, pages 1 to 3, 17 and 18 (printed page equals PDF page less two).

WHAT TO ASK ANDY

Request 7. Whether any financing in the case is labelled or certified green or sustainability-linked, at what yield or spread compared with an unlabelled equivalent, and who certified it. One data point of this kind would test the model of slide 17 directly.

title: Climate-Related Disclosure: Four Pillars
notes:
THE TABLE

The structure of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures, Final Report, June 2017, Figure 4 on printed page 14: four recommendations (governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics and targets) supported by eleven recommended disclosures. The cells are my shortening of the wording in the report.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

The Task Force divided climate-related risks into two categories, transition risks (policy and legal, technology, market and reputation) and physical risks, event-driven (acute) or longer-term shifts in climate patterns (chronic) (pages 5 and 6). Its list of policy responses includes encouraging greater water efficiency measures (page 4), and its account of physical risk says financial performance may be affected by changes in water availability, sourcing and quality (page 6). Strategy disclosure (c) asks organisations to describe the resilience of their strategy under different climate-related scenarios, including a 2 degrees Celsius or lower scenario, which is the item that links disclosure to the protection and discounting questions of the focus part. Metrics and targets (b) asks for scope 1, scope 2 and, if appropriate, scope 3 greenhouse gas emissions.

CAUTIONS

The PDF I retrieved carries a legend 'draft for discussion purposes only' on its first page, although it is the final report of June 2017, so check the final text before quoting. I could not retrieve IFRS S2, the later standard that carries the recommendations into reporting (the download was a sign-in page), so the slide describes the Task Force structure and not the current requirement; check IFRS S2 and national rules before telling students what is mandatory. The Week 6 deck covers how unlisted assets report to investors, and these slides do not repeat that.

SOURCE

Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (2017), Final Report: Recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures, June 2017, Figure 4 on page 14, and pages 5 and 6 (printed pages).

WHAT TO ASK ANDY

Request 8. Which reporting framework the institutions in the case use for climate and water (a TCFD-aligned report, ISSB, a national requirement, none), what metrics they report for water (withdrawal, consumption, stress exposure) and whether anyone assures them. The strategy item on scenario resilience is the one to ask about.

title: Water as a Financial Stability Risk
notes:
THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

On 21 and 22 May 2026 the Banco de España hosted at its Madrid headquarters a high-level meeting, Water and financial stability: moving from risks to resilience, convened jointly by the OECD, the Network of Central Banks and Supervisors for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) and CDP, as part of the work of the OECD Roundtable on Financing Water. It was to analyse the macroeconomic and financial risks stemming from water scarcity, variability and quality, and to bring together senior representatives of central banks and financial authorities, international organisations, financial institutions, business and insurance, and academics. The agenda was to address sectoral vulnerabilities, sovereign exposure, price stability implications, supervisory responses and the insurance protection gaps associated with water-related risks, and the meeting sought to advance understanding of water as a systemic financial stability risk (Banco de España press release, Madrid, 20 May 2026).

WHY IT IS ON THE SLIDE

This is the point where the first hour meets the case. The earlier slides show how risk enters prices (slide 5), how it is scored (slide 6) and how it is reported (slide 10). The meeting shows the supervisory question that follows, which is whether water risk is a risk to the financial system as well as to an asset. The OECD page for the meeting says it drew on the recommendations of the OECD publication Embedding Water-related Risks in Financial Stability Frameworks; I could not retrieve that publication, so the slide cites only the press release.

THE PROGRAMME NAMED ON THE SLIDE

title: Data Centres and Environmental Damages
notes:
THE FIGURE

Muller (2026), NBER Working Paper 35100, Table 2: gross external damages from the electricity used by operational data centres in 2025, divided by the 2024 GDP of the data processing, hosting and related services industry in the same state. North Dakota 5.51 (damages USD 665 million, industry GDP USD 121 million), Wyoming 2.15 (244 and 114), Iowa 0.76 (1,440 and 1,904), Oklahoma 0.57 (456 and 805), Virginia 0.31 (4,290 and 13,952), all states 0.05 (24,600 and 544,148). Each ratio is damages divided by the state's industry GDP, so a value above 1 means the damages exceed the industry's output in that state.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

Using facility-level data for about 2,800 operational data centres in 2025, the paper estimates that they consume roughly 250 TWh, about 5 to 6 per cent of US generation, and that the electricity generation to supply them causes about USD 25 billion of gross external damages from local air pollution and greenhouse gases, with a range of USD 10 to 33 billion (abstract). Local air pollution is valued with the AP4 integrated assessment model and greenhouse gases with a social cost of carbon of about USD 190 a tonne, with about USD 50 as the alternative (page 8). Texas and Virginia account for 30 per cent of the national damage, and data centres in ten states produce 70 per cent (page 4). Planned facilities would add USD 21 billion, roughly the damages of the operating fleet in the third quarter of 2025, so damages could rise by up to 85 per cent in the near term (abstract and page 4). Set against an assumed 0.5 per cent productivity boost to GDP from AI, the damages attributable to AI are 2.4 per cent of the gain (page 4), a provisional calculation the author labels as such. The environmental aspect of the data-centre thread is incidence, who bears the cost and where, which is a question about externalities and not about financing.

CAUTIONS

The damages come from electricity generation, not from the data centres' own emissions or their water use. The ratio compares damages with the output of one industry, which is a small base in the states at the top of the table, so it is large where the industry is small, and the denominator should be stated whenever the ratio is quoted. The estimate depends heavily on the social cost of carbon, which varies by a factor of almost four between the two values used. This is an April 2026 NBER working paper and has not been through peer review. Water is not covered. For water, Li, Yang, Islam and Ren (Communications of the ACM, 2025) set out the three scopes in which a water footprint is reported: scope 1 on-site cooling, scope 2 water used to generate the electricity, and scope 3 supply chain water, and estimate that training GPT-3 in Microsoft's US data centres could consume 5.4 million litres of water, of which 700,000 litres is on-site (page 2 of the PDF). The scope distinction is the one the TCFD asks for in emissions. Ramboll's 2025 whitepaper on sustainable data centres, filed beside the Week 2 material, proposes benchmarks and has not been used here.

SOURCE

(2026), Measuring the impact of data centers in the United States economy: monetary damage from air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions, NBER Working Paper 35100, April 2026, abstract and pages 4, 8 and 17 (Table 2). title: Flexible Data Centres and the Grid
notes:
THE FIGURE

Knittel, Senga and Wang (2025), NBER Working Paper 34065, July 2025, a model of three US power systems (Mid-Atlantic, Texas and WECC). Left panel: projected 2030 data-centre load growth, compared with a system with no growth, raises annual CO2 emissions by 47 million tonnes (20 per cent) in the Mid-Atlantic, 55 (58 per cent) in Texas and 46 (24 per cent) in WECC (page 8). Right panel: the largest change in system emissions when data centres can shift their load in time, which is up to 40 per cent lower in Texas, where wind and solar are projected to supply 54 per cent of generation, and up to 3 per cent higher in the Mid-Atlantic and WECC (pages 2 and 3).

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

Data centres typically run at about 80 per cent utilisation, which leaves headroom to shift work, especially for training workloads (page 1). Across all regions and price scenarios, temporal flexibility lowers total system costs, by up to 4 per cent in the Mid-Atlantic, 5 per cent in Texas and 2 per cent in WECC (page 12). The effect on emissions depends on which of two forces dominates. Flexibility facilitates renewable integration by moving load to hours of abundant wind and solar, and it also improves the utilisation of baseload plants. Where renewables are cheap and plentiful the first dominates, and where they are scarcer the second does and coal plants that would have retired can run more steadily (pages 2 and 3). In a counterfactual with renewable costs at 1.3 times the base, Texas's renewable share falls to 21 per cent, coal stays on the system and the emissions advantage of flexibility disappears (page 3). The environmental aspect on this slide is the conditional one. Whether a data centre's behaviour is good for the environment depends on the grid it sits on, which, on my reading, makes a rule that treats all data centres alike a poor instrument.

CAUTIONS

This is a system model of 2030 with assumed load, not an observation. The abstract's cost savings and the headline emissions figures are the largest values across the scenarios, and the paper reports ranges, so the slide says 'at most'. It covers temporal shifting only and does not cover locational shifting or water.

SOURCE

title: Three Models for Long-Lived Assets
notes:
THE TABLE

The focus of the hour is one question seen from three sides. A long-lived infrastructure asset has an environmental dimension, and three things decide what it is worth to an investor or a public body: what the market pays for the sustainability it offers, how the benefits that arrive in the distant future are discounted, and what protection against rare losses earns in avoided damage. Each has a model and each model has an interactive page that opens on a generic setting. None of them is about water, and each of them is something a water case can test.

THE THREE MODELS

Pastor, Stambaugh and Taylor (2021) is an equilibrium model in which some investors have a taste for green holdings. It predicts lower expected returns on greener assets, a tilt in portfolios and a return given up by the tilting investors (slides 16 and 17). The survey slides give it evidence in both directions: the green bond premium of 6 basis points (slide 9) and the carbon premium in the opposite sign (slide 8), against the disagreement of the raters that the model needs to agree on greenness (slides 3 and 4).

The discounting model is the Treasury's declining schedule, its sensitivity case and the June 2026 independent review, with gamma discounting as the way uncertainty about the rate lowers the long-run rate (slides 18 and 19). It predicts that the answer to a question about a century of benefit depends mostly on the schedule, while a project with early benefits hardly notices.

The expected-loss model is a loss curve with a protection standard, a drift in frequency and exposure, and a discount regime (slides 20 and 21). It predicts a net benefit that rises and then falls with the standard, with an optimum that moves with the tail of the curve, the drift and the schedule. The Aqueduct decomposition of risk into hazard, exposure and vulnerability (slide 6) and the Lifelines benefit-cost range (slide 7) frame it.

HOW THEY FIT

The first answers the question of who is willing to pay for a sustainable asset, the second whether the benefit of a resilient asset arrives soon enough to count, and the third how large that benefit is. Students should leave able to put the same three questions to any sustainability case.

RETURN TO THIS IN THE CASE

The case should supply evidence for each of the three: a price or a spread that reflects the environmental dimension (Request 7), the appraisal rules used (Request 6), and a hazard, a loss and a cost for a protection option (Requests 3, 4 and 5). If the case can supply only one of them, the discounting page is the one that needs the least data.

title: Pastor, Stambaugh and Taylor (2021): Tastes and Prices
notes:
THE ARGUMENT OF THE SLIDE

Pastor, Stambaugh and Taylor (2021), Sustainable investing in equilibrium, derive three results from a mean-variance model in which some investors have a taste for green holdings. Investor i gets a nonpecuniary benefit of d(i) times the ESG score g(n) from each unit held of asset n (page 6). Portfolio weights are X(i) = (1/a) times the inverse covariance matrix times (mu + (d(i) times g)/a), with a the relative risk aversion (equation 4, page 6), and clearing the market with the wealth-weighted mean taste d-bar gives mu = a times the covariance matrix times the market weights minus (d-bar/a) times g (equations 5 and 6, pages 7 and 8). Assuming the market portfolio is ESG-neutral gives Proposition 1: expected excess returns are the CAPM return minus (d-bar/a) times g (equation 9, page 8), so the CAPM alpha of asset n is minus (d-bar/a) times g(n) (Corollary 2, equation 10, page 9). Proposition 3 gives portfolios: investor i holds the market plus (delta(i)/a squared) times the inverse covariance matrix times g, with delta(i) the taste less the mean (equation 14, page 10).

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

Greener assets have negative alphas and browner assets positive ones, because the price carries the taste. Investors with above-average taste tilt towards the green portfolio, and below-average investors, including those with no taste, tilt away from it, so holding the market is optimal only for the average investor (page 10). If all investors have the same taste, all hold the market, and the alphas are still there (Corollary 4, page 11), so that dispersion in tastes is what an ESG investment industry needs. The authors show that expected utility in equilibrium rises with the square of the deviation of an investor's taste from the average (equation 13, page 9). The third result, which the next slide draws, is that the expected return of investor i is the market's less delta(i) times d-bar times the quadratic form g'Σ⁻¹g divided by a cubed. This is my derivation from equations 9 and 14. The page checks it against the direct calculation.

CAUTIONS

One period, mean-variance preferences, tastes taken as known and a common view of which assets are green. Footnote 4 of the paper says the results hold if investors disagree about the scores, with the score replaced by a wealth-weighted average (page 9), but disagreement between raters of the size slide 3 shows would weaken the effect and is not modelled. The paper's own sections on ESG as a risk factor and on social impact are not on the slide. The published version is the Journal of Financial Economics 142(2), 550 to 571; the page numbers are those of NBER Working Paper 26549.

SOURCE

Pastor, L., Stambaugh, R. F. and Taylor, L. A. (2021), Sustainable investing in equilibrium, Journal of Financial Economics 142(2), 550 to 571; NBER Working Paper 26549, pages 6 to 11 (printed page equals PDF page less two).

RETURN TO THIS IN THE CASE

The model is a test of whether the sustainability of the asset in the case is priced, and the data it needs are small: one spread, yield or valuation for the asset or its financing against a comparable asset that does not offer the same environmental feature, and the identity of the marginal buyer (Request 7). If the case shows no price effect, the model's own explanation is the absence of dispersion in tastes or the noise in the scores of slides 3 and 4.

THE FIGURE

title: The Treasury Discount Rate and Its Schedules
notes:
THE TABLE

The forward discount rates, per cent, in the Treasury's February 2026 guidance and in the June 2026 independent review. Green Book supplementary guidance on discounting, paragraph 3.1 and Table 3.A, page 12: 3.5 for years 1 to 30, 3.0 for years 31 to 75 and 2.5 for years 76 to 125. The sensitivity case without pure time preference, Table 3.B, page 13: 3.00, 2.57, 2.14 and then 1.71, 1.29 and 0.86 for years 126 to 200, 201 to 300 and beyond 300 (the table on the slide stops at year 125). Freeman and Groom (2026), Table 1, page 2 of 15: standard projects 3.0, 2.5 and 2.25; social insurance projects 1.5, 1.0 and 0.75.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

The Treasury's rate is a social time preference rate, rho plus mu times g, with rho = delta + L: pure time preference of 0.5 per cent, an allowance for catastrophic risk of 1 per cent, and a wealth effect of the elasticity of marginal utility, 1, times growth in consumption per head, 2 per cent, which sums to 3.5 per cent (guidance paragraphs 2.1 to 2.4, page 7; review paragraph 7, page 4 of 15). For horizons beyond 50 years the guidance also asks for a sensitivity run with pure time preference removed (paragraphs 3.3 to 3.5, pages 12 and 13). The review recommends a flatter schedule, 3.0 falling to 2.25, because the standard model of consumption growth cannot produce a strongly declining rate from the UK data and only structural uncertainty about the growth regime does (paragraphs 43 to 46, page 10 of 15), and a second schedule for projects with significant social insurance properties, interventions against severe downside risks to society whose benefits arrive when marginal utility is high, with a risk premium of minus 0.5 per cent (paragraph 60, page 12 of 15). The gamma case is the textbook way uncertainty about the rate lowers it with the horizon. If the right rate is gamma distributed with mean mu and standard deviation sigma, the rate applied to year t is mu divided by one plus sigma squared times t over mu. That is my derivation from the gamma moment generating function; Weitzman (2001), the source of the idea, was not retrieved. The survey of climate finance reaches the same kind of result by another route, since the sign of the risk premium on assets that hedge climate damage depends on whether the uncertainty is about the climate or about the economy (slide 5).

CAUTIONS

The review is an independent report commissioned by HM Treasury and is not Treasury policy; the February 2026 guidance is. The two disagree about one thing that bears on this slide: the review recommends that discount-rate sensitivity analysis not be undertaken (page 2 of 15), while the guidance requires it beyond 50 years (paragraph 3.4). Whether a resilience measure qualifies as social insurance is a judgement for HM Treasury, and the mapping from the review's examples (pandemic preparedness, counter-terrorism) to climate resilience is mine, not the review's. The tables stop at 125 years, beyond which the review recommends explicit welfare analysis.

SOURCE

HM Treasury (2026), Green Book supplementary guidance: discounting, February 2026, pages 7, 12 and 13; Freeman, M. C. and Groom, B. (2026), Green Book Discount Rate Review: summary of findings and recommendations, 30 June 2026, pages 2, 4, 10 to 12 (page n of 15).

RETURN TO THIS IN THE CASE

Every appraisal in the case uses some discount rate and some horizon, and the rule that set them (a treasury, a regulator, a lender or the investor's hurdle rate) is part of the case (Request 6). The question for the second hour is which row of this table the case's appraisal belongs in, and what would have happened under another.

title: Expected Annual Loss and Protection
notes:
THE ARGUMENT OF THE SLIDE

The third model is the simplest calculation of what a resilience measure earns. Let p be the probability in a year of an event at least as bad as a given one, so an event with return period T has p = 1 over T. The loss from an event with return period T is L(T), the loss of the 100-year event times (T over 100) to the power s. The expected annual loss is the area under the loss against p, which for a power curve has a closed form. Events more frequent than one in two years and rarer than one in a thousand years are left out. A measure with a standard of R years removes the losses of all events up to R, so the loss it avoids is the part of the area to the right of 1 over R. The avoided loss grows over the years as events become more frequent and the value exposed grows, by (1 plus gamma times t) times (1 plus e) to the power t. The present value of the avoided losses, discounted on one of the regimes of slide 18, is compared with the capital cost, which rises with the standard as (R over 20) to the power kappa, and with upkeep.

THE LINK TO THE EVIDENCE

Aqueduct decomposes risk into hazard, exposure and vulnerability and gives the risk element of the baseline water stress indicator as R = H x E x V (pages 10 and 11), and the loss curve folds exposure and vulnerability into the loss and keeps the hazard as the probability. Lifelines supplies the reference range for the benefit-cost ratio of strengthening infrastructure: above 1 in 96 per cent of 3,000 scenarios, above 6 in 25 per cent, and a median that doubles when climate change is counted (Overview, page 12). The Treasury's review treats projects that pay off in times of societal decline separately from standard projects (slide 18). The loss curve, the protection rule and the cost curve are mine, chosen to be as simple as the argument allows, and no number in the model is an estimate.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

Net benefit rises and then falls with the standard, because the first increments of protection remove frequent small losses cheaply and the later ones remove rare large losses at a cost that rises faster than the loss avoided. The optimum standard moves with three things the case may be able to inform: how steep the loss curve is, how fast frequency and exposure are rising, and how the future is discounted.

CAUTIONS

The curve has no uncertainty about its own shape, no interaction between events, and no failure of the measure beyond its standard. Real loss curves come from hazard and damage models. The result is a ceiling on what a real appraisal would find. The benefit is avoided loss only and leaves out any benefit in ordinary years.

SOURCE

Kuzma and co-authors (2023), Aqueduct 4.0, pages 10 and 11; Hallegatte, Rentschler and Rozenberg (2019), Lifelines, Overview, page 12; the model is the author's (models_w7.py).

RETURN TO THIS IN THE CASE

The three inputs the model needs from a real case are a loss for a stated event or scenario, a cost and life for a protection option, and the rules for discounting. Those are Requests 4, 5 and 6, and they are the ones to press for.

notes:

THE FIGURE

The generic setting of the page: a loss of 100 million from a one-in-100-year event, a steepness of 0.5, frequency rising 0.5 per cent a year and exposed value 1 per cent a year, a cost of 60 million for a one-in-20 standard rising with the standard to the power 0.6, upkeep of 1.5 per cent of cost a year, 60 years of benefit, discounted on the Green Book schedule. Left panel: the loss from an event against its return period on a logarithmic axis, with the protected range shaded for a standard of one in 50. A one-in-50-year event costs 71 million and a one-in-1,000-year event 316 million. The expected annual loss is 13.5 million, of which a one-in-50 standard avoids 11.3 and leaves 2.2 from events beyond it. Right panel: net present value against the standard. At one in 50 the benefit-cost ratio is 2.81 and the net present value 259 million, and the best of 40 standards tried is about one in 29, with 268 million. About 37 per cent of the present value of benefits falls after year 30. Under the six discount regimes the ratio at one in 50 runs from 2.75 to 4.17.

WHAT THE PAGE ADDS

Presets: the generic setting; a heavy tail with fast drift (a 100-year loss of 200 million, steepness 0.8, frequency rising 2 per cent a year), where the best standard moves to about one in 67; and the conventional case with no drift and a flat 3.5 per cent. On the generic inputs, the social insurance schedule moves the best standard to about one in 42. A fourth chart shows the avoided loss in each year with and without the drift. The numbers in the preset are illustrative, not estimates, and are not anyone's case.

HOW IT WAS BUILT

Python (models_w7.py) and JavaScript agree on 300 random settings to 13 decimal places (check_models_w7.py), and the page was checked against the Python values for the three presets.

QUESTIONS FOR THE CLASS

Which of the three, the steeper curve, the faster drift or the lower discount rate, moves the best standard most? Then ask what an appraiser has to show in order to use the social insurance schedule at all.

RETURN TO THIS IN THE CASE

The page is the frame for the case discussion on the protection or adaptation choice in the case: a hazard (Request 3), a loss (Request 4), options with cost and life (Request 5) and the appraisal rule (Request 6). The best use of the second hour is to replace the generic numbers by the case's, one at a time, and watch the best standard move.

title: Three Models Compared
notes:
THE TABLE

The synthesis slide of the focus part and, if time is short, the one to keep. Each model answers a different question about the same long-lived asset, and an investor or a public body needs all three answers before it commits.

Pastor, Stambaugh and Taylor (2021) explains what the market pays for sustainability. It predicts that greener assets earn lower returns and carry a higher price, that investors who care give up return, and that the effect needs dispersion in tastes. The evidence is mixed. Baker and co-authors find a green municipal bond premium of about 6 basis points (slide 9), and Bolton and Kacperczyk find a premium for emitters (slide 8) that fits the model's brown side, but Berg and co-authors show raters disagree, which weakens the signal investors can act on (slides 3 and 4). Its limit is one period, known tastes and a common view of which assets are green.

The Treasury schedules, the review and gamma discounting explain how a distant benefit is valued. They predict that the schedule matters most for projects whose benefit arrives late. The evidence is the schedules themselves, the review's finding that only structural uncertainty about growth gives a strongly declining term structure, and the survey of climate finance on the sign of the risk premium. Its limit is that the guidance and the review disagree on sensitivity analysis and that the tables stop at 125 years.

The expected-loss model explains what protection earns. It predicts a net benefit that peaks at a standard moving with the tail, the drift and the schedule. The reference range is Lifelines (benefit-cost above 1 in 96 per cent of scenarios), and its limit is that the curve is assumed, not estimated.

HOW THE THREE FIT

They give three tests of an environmental claim for an asset. Is anyone paying for it, and who? Does the benefit arrive soon enough to count under the rule that is used? Is the loss it prevents large enough, and does the standard chosen make sense? A case that passes one only should be questioned.

THE LINK TO THE CASE

Students should arrive at the case able to put each test to a real asset. The case section lists the evidence each test needs, in priority order. The discussion in the second hour is where they are applied.

RETURN TO THIS IN THE CASE

Take the three tests to the case and ask which can be run with the data on the table, which need one more number, and which cannot be run.

title: Case Study: Water Infrastructure and the Environmental Dimension of ESG (Andreas Jobst, Central Bank of the UAE)
notes:
AN OUTLINE ONLY

By design this is one slide naming the ground the case covers and leaving the discussion to the guest, Andreas Jobst, Chief (Monetary Policy) at the Central Bank of the UAE according to his one-page CV, and a member of the Global Infrastructure Advisory Panel. It states no facts about the case, takes no position and makes no claim, so it cannot spoil what he says. The title is a working title: it gives the subject Helen named (water infrastructure and the E of ESG) and nothing else. His employer and title are as on his CV; confirm how he wishes to be introduced.

THE FIVE HEADINGS

The setting and the decision; the institution; water risk and data; the financial question; and discussion with the guest. They are neutral and could stand over any case on a water asset.

HOW THE WEEK PREPARES THE CASE

The first hour is deliberately broader than the case. It shows how sustainability is measured and how raters disagree (slides 3 and 4), how climate and water risk show up in prices (5 to 7), what carbon and green labels earn (8 and 9), how firms disclose and how supervisors are beginning to treat water (10 to 12), and what data centres cost the environment (13 and 14). The focus part gives three models, with pages: what the market pays for sustainability, how a distant benefit is discounted and what protection earns (15 to 22). Students should leave with three tests they can put to any environmental claim. The second hour applies them to one real case.

Tier 1, needed before anything else can be built.

Request 4. Exposure and loss: asset values, how services depend on them, and any loss or outage estimate per event or scenario. Feeds: slides 7, 20 and 21. Tests: expected loss. Sensitivity: commercial or supervisory; one worked figure for a stated event would do.
Request 5. The resilience or adaptation options considered, with capital cost, upkeep and life. Feeds: slides 20 and 21. Tests: expected loss. Sensitivity: commercial.

Tier 3, evidence on markets, reporting and supervision.
